The government's position on judicial appointments is constitutionally sound and reflects the democratic mandate of the elected executive. The collegium system — invented by judges for judges — has no textual basis in the Constitution. The people of India voted for accountability, not judicial oligarchy. Returning files for reconsideration is a legitimate exercise of executive review, not obstruction. The real question is: why should unelected judges have absolute, unreviewable power over their own appointments? The NJAC Act, passed with near-unanimous parliamentary support, was the democratic answer. Its unconstitutional striking down by the Supreme Court was itself an act of institutional overreach. The government is right to push back. #JudicialAccountability #DemocraticMandate #NJACWasRight #ConstitutionalBalance

The proposed net-metering policy revision by MNRE is actually a step in the right direction if you read the fine print. A 24-month grandfather clause for existing installations would have been the sensible middle path. This is what the CERC public consultation should have surfaced.

He said the original stormwater drain network for this zone was designed in 1987 for a population of 40,000. Today the ward has 2.8 lakh residents. The drain capacity was never upgraded. I work as a civil engineer and I want to explain what's actually happening here technically so people understand the scale of failure. The water mains in these wards are pre-1980 asbestos cement pipes. AC pipes have a design life of 30-40 years. They are now 45+ years old. When pressure drops at night (which it does in every Indian city due to intermittent supply), negative pressure sucks in surrounding groundwater — which in dense urban areas is heavily contaminated by leaking sewer lines running in the same utility corridor. Thread on what actually happened in Vasundhara Enclave flooding (1/7): The storm drain running parallel to the main road was encroached upon by a builder who constructed a commercial complex directly over it in 2018. MCD gave NOC. Town planning department gave NOC. Nobody checked the structural impact on drainage capacity. (2/7) The drain's cross-section was reduced by nearly 60%. Every monsoon since then, backflow happens. This year rainfall was 340mm in 6 hours — the drain simply couldn't handle it. (3/7) Desilting contract was awarded in March. Work was supposed to be completed by May 15. As of July, contractor had done maybe 20% of the stretch. No penalty clause was invoked. (4/7) The audit trail shows payments were released at 80% completion milestone — which was falsely certified by the junior engineer. This is textbook corruption. (5/7) Three transformer units in the area are 28 years old. DISCOM had flagged replacement in their 2020 capex plan. Budget was allocated. Equipment was never procured. Money was diverted. (6/7) So last night when water hit those transformers — it was entirely predictable. The explosions were not an accident. They were the inevitable result of compounded institutional failure. (7/7) We need: HC petition, CBI audit of desilting contracts, criminal FIR against the builder who encroached the drain, and immediate suspension of the certifying JE. RT if you agree.

Thread on why the Governor's early release order is constitutionally suspect (1/6): Article 161 grants pardoning power but Supreme Court in Maru Ram v. Union of India held this must be exercised on aid and advice of Council of Ministers, NOT unilaterally. (2/6) Here the CM's office claims they recommended remission. But the Prison Advisory Board — a statutory body under the Prisons Act — had flagged 'conduct concerns' in its last two reviews. (3/6) The question is: can the executive override a statutory advisory body's recommendation? Short answer: legally murky. (4/6) The habeas corpus petition filed by the victim's family is actually the stronger route here — they're arguing the continued detention was lawful and the release is the violation. Inverted habeas. Interesting. (5/6) Precedent: Laxman Naskar v. Union of India laid down 5 factors for remission. Has ANY of those been publicly demonstrated here? (6/6) This will likely go to a division bench. Watch this space.

I am a civil engineer and I want to explain what happened technically so people understand the real failure here. Basement libraries in Delhi's coaching belt are almost universally non-compliant. The National Building Code 2016 explicitly prohibits habitable use of basements below natural ground level without certified waterproofing, sump pumps, and dual-exit compliance. The MCD building plan approval process requires a structural safety certificate AND a drainage NOC from the Delhi Jal Board. If either is forged, the entire occupancy certificate is void. The institute was operating an ILLEGAL commercial space. The students sitting there had no idea they were in an uncertified death trap. This is systemic, not a one-off.

Quick thread on what actually happened at the Poisar-Kandivali transmission main (1/4): The 45-year-old ductile iron pipe had been operating beyond its design life since 2019. Multiple patch repairs visible on Google Earth imagery from 2021 onwards. (2/4): The booster pump station at Pump House No. 7 had a faulty pressure relief valve — this was noted in the March 2024 maintenance log but the replacement part was 'pending procurement' for 14 months. (3/4): On the night of the burst, the duty valve operator was not at his post. The automated SCADA alert went to a WhatsApp group that nobody was monitoring at 2am. (4/4): By the time manual shutdown was initiated, 40 million litres had already discharged into the surrounding area. This is systemic failure, not bad luck.
